William of Ockham
wĭl´yam ŏv ŏk´am
n. (William of Ockham, c. 1287–1347, English Franciscan, the greatest of the nominalists, whose via moderna shaped the schools in which Luther was trained)
From Ockham in Surrey; the maxim called Ockham's razor — that explanations should not multiply entities needlessly — is named for him.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

William of Ockham denied that universals have any existence outside the mind: only individuals are real, and a general term is a sign standing for many singulars. From this he drew consequences that ran through the late Middle Ages. Knowledge of God by natural reason is far weaker than Aquinas allowed, so revelation must carry more weight — a conclusion with a Protestant flavour. God's will is not bound by any order of natures, so what is right is right because He wills it, and He could by His absolute power do otherwise than He has ordained. He also fought a long political battle against Pope John XXII over apostolic poverty and papal authority, was excommunicated, and wrote in defence of the empire against papal claims. The doctrine of God he bequeathed has a true centre: Eph 1:11 says God “worketh all things after the counsel of his own will,” and Psa 115:3 that “he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased.” Isa 46:10 and Dan 4:35 say the same. What his school added was a doctrine of justification in which man, by doing what is in him, disposes himself for grace — the very scheme the young Luther was taught and later repudiated.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the nominalists as a sect of school philosophers, the followers of Ockham, who maintained that universals have no real existence, but are mere names or words.

expand to see more

NOM'INALIST, n. One of a sect of school philosophers, the followers of Occam or Ockham, who maintained that universals have no real existence, but are mere names or words.

SOV'EREIGNTY, n. Supreme power; supremacy; the possession of the highest power, or of uncontrollable power.

WILL, n. Choice; determination; the faculty by which we determine either to do or forbear.

Key Scripture

Eph 1:11 — "In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:"

Psa 115:3 — "But our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased."

Isa 46:10 — "Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:"

Dan 4:35 — "And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?"

Modern Corruption

Ockham's school taught that a man who does what lies in him will be given grace, and that sentence is the one Luther had to be delivered from.

expand to see more

The late nominalist formula — facere quod in se est, to do what is in oneself — held that God in His ordained power will not deny grace to the man who does his natural best. It is Semi-Pelagianism with a voluntarist foundation, and it was the working doctrine of the schools at Erfurt where Luther studied. He tried it, and found that a conscience which takes the law seriously can never know whether it has done its best; the terror of that uncertainty drove him to Rom 1:17. Tit 3:5 and Rom 4:4 had already settled it: grace that answers a man's best effort is wages, not grace.

The second caution concerns the razor and its modern use. As a rule for framing explanations it is sound and still serviceable. As a metaphysical principle it was pressed into a denial that natural reason can establish much about God at all, and the long effect was to divide faith from knowledge — a separation the modern mind inherited and widened, so that doctrine is now commonly treated as a value rather than a truth claim. The Reformed answer keeps both: God's sovereign will is absolutely free, Eph 1:11 is a statement of fact, and what He has revealed is knowledge.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek boule (G1012), counsel, deliberate purpose; energeo (G1754), to work effectually; Hebrew chaphets (H2654), to please.

expand to see more

Greek boule (G1012) — counsel, settled purpose; Ephesians 1:11.

Greek proorizo (G4309) — to predestinate, to mark out beforehand; Ephesians 1:11.

Hebrew chaphets (H2654) — to delight, to please; Psalm 115:3.

Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel, advice; Isaiah 46:10.

Aramaic tsaba (H6634) — to will, to desire; Daniel 4:35.

Usage

"“worketh all things after the counsel of his own will” (Eph 1:11) — the true centre of his doctrine of God."

"“he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased” (Psa 115:3) — sovereignty without constraint."

"“My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure” (Isa 46:10) — the decree that does not fail."
